title: Policy Provisions on Unpaid Premium: the Grace Period, Lapse and Putting a Policy Back in Force
content:
A supplement premium unpaid after its due date puts a policy under Medicare Supplement Insurance Policies into its grace period, during which benefits carry on exactly as before and claims are paid.

### When the policy lapses

The plan has not received the outstanding premium by the last day of the grace period counted from the date the unpaid premium fell due. The clock starts from the date the unpaid premium fell due, as the policy's premium account shows it, and it is read against the policy and the entry together, before the lapse is recorded. Calendar days are counted from the day after the due date, every day of the week counts, the last day of the grace period is itself inside it, and full 24-hour periods are never used in place of calendar days. The length of the grace period is the number of calendar days the plan letter carries.

Where the grace period runs 31 calendar days, a payment reaching the plan on the thirty-first day after the due date arrives on the last day of the grace period and the policy has not lapsed; where nothing has reached the plan once that day has ended, it has.

### Where the premium arrives in time

Where the outstanding premium reaches the plan before that day ends the policy continues unbroken, with no new waiting period and no fresh health questions.

### What a lapse does to benefits

A policy that lapses stops paying benefits for services on or after its end date, and claims for services before it are still paid.

### Reinstatement

A lapsed policy may be put back in force inside the plan letter's reinstatement window on the evidence the letter requires, and reinstatement restores the original effective date so that no new waiting period begins.

After that window the policyholder must apply afresh and may be underwritten, and the plan says so plainly rather than letting the policyholder assume they can pay their way back in.
